root.claim: A single deterministic fixed-tape Turing machine multiplies two $n$-bit integers exactly in $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ time with $\kappa=2^{-182}$.
root.method: Replace the logarithmic number of full scans of Fourier-transform multiplication by two power-saving tape procedures, build an exact convolution-based multiplier around them, and add up the costs

motivation.text: Scanning $\Theta(n)$ bits at each of $\Theta(\log n)$ transform levels already costs $\Theta(n\log n)$, so both the data movement and the butterfly arithmetic must be made cheaper than one scan per level.

quote.quote: We therefore need savings in both movement and arithmetic.

root.salient: The saving is a strict power of the logarithm, $(\lg n)^{-\kappa}$, although the exponent $\kappa=2^{-182}$ is astronomically small; the bound holds through all input lengths.

adds.name: input length
adds.meaning: The number of bits of each of the two integers to be multiplied.

adds.name: saving exponent
adds.meaning: The fixed constant $2^{-182}$ by which the power of the logarithm is lowered.

adds.name: interchange exponent
adds.meaning: A fixed exponent below one: the cost per bit of interchanging two address fields of width u is u to this power.

children.claim: Interchanging two disjoint contiguous $u$-bit address fields of an array of volume $V$ takes $O(Vu^\tau)$ time for a fixed $\tau<1$, by recursing through a network of $W$ wires and $m$-dimensional labels that makes only $s<Wm$ smaller interchanges.
children.method: Build a fixed linear network whose edge changes cost rank-many smaller interchanges, and solve the resulting rank-deficit recursion

motivation.text: An edge change of rank $a$ costs $a$ smaller interchanges, and because the total rank is below the number of wires times $m$, the recursion on chunk width grows only by a power less than one.

quote.quote: Because the sum of these ranks is less than the number of wires times $m$, the resulting recurrence saves a power of the chunk width.

children.salient: Although the final effect is an exact permutation, the intermediate steps are XOR combinations of data, and the cost per bit grows only as $u^\tau$ with $\tau<1$, not as $\log V$.

adds.name: field width
adds.meaning: The number of bits in each of the two address fields being interchanged.

adds.name: array volume
adds.meaning: The number of data bits stored in the array.

adds.name: wire count
adds.meaning: The number of wires of the fixed linear network.

adds.name: label dimension
adds.meaning: The dimension of the fixed space whose subspaces label the network.

adds.name: smaller calls
adds.meaning: The total rank of all edge changes, which is the number of smaller interchanges one use of the network makes.

children.claim: Splitting, merging and fixed permutations of digits of an array stored in lexicographic address order cost $O(V)$ by linear scans on a fixed number of tapes.

quote.quote: Each of the following operations on an array of volume $V$ takes $O(V)$ steps on a fixed number of one-dimensional tapes:

children.claim: Adding to a later address field an offset computed from earlier fields, or multiplying it by a fixed unit modulo $q^b$, costs $O(V)$.

quote.quote: Suppose a target field $y\in[Q]$ follows its control fields, each control used in an offset having $O(b)$ digits.

children.claim: A fixed linear network of copy, gather, scatter and side-injection gates on banks $X,Y$ and scratch wires sends $(X,Y)$ to $(-Y,X)$ in three stages and restores arbitrary initial scratch values.
children.salient: The exchange works whatever the scratch wires held at the start, and leaves them exactly as they were: a first pair of rows cancels the old scratch contents, later rows add the wanted contribution, and the last rows undo the scratch changes.

quote.quote: For arbitrary initial values of its auxiliary wires, a forward invocation changes $y_S$ to $y_S+x_S$ and leaves every other value unchanged.

children.claim: If each vertex $v$ of the network carries an invertible operator $D_v$ so that stored arrays are $D_v$ applied to logical arrays, pointwise gates commute with the common frame and the network implements $D_{\rm out}\,\mathsf S\,D_{\rm in}^{-1}$, leaving only the edge changes $D_vD_u^{-1}$ to pay for.

quote.quote: Thus the common frame commutes with the pointwise gate, and the invariant continues to the sinks.

children.claim: Nested nondegenerate subspaces of an $m$-dimensional space attached to the gates and terminals make the only dimension losses the central-wire returns, so the total rank of the edge changes satisfies $s<Wm$.
children.salient: The total rank is strictly below the number of wires times $m$: only the central wires ever lose dimension, so the loss is less than half the source dimension, and this strict gap is the whole source of the power saving.

quote.quote: Every edge joins comparable nondegenerate labels. The only decreasing edges are the central-wire edges from time 3 to time 4; their dimension loss is $h$.

children.claim: The $\mathbb F_2$ network with $W_{\rm b}$ wires and rational labels has endpoint matrices differing by the identity on every input role, which gives the address shear $H\leftarrow H+D$ on every role at total edge rank $s_{\rm b}<W_{\rm b}m$.
children.salient: The endpoint matrices differ by the same identity matrix on every input role, scratch roles included, so one and the same shear $H\leftarrow H+D$ is applied to all $W_{\rm b}$ role arrays.

quote.quote: The bit network has $W_{\rm b}$ wires, uses only pointwise XOR gates, and sends its input vector to the permutation $\rho$ of that vector.

children.claim: Every rational matrix $A$ of rank $a$ equals $E_1\Pi E_2$ with $E_1,E_2$ invertible lower triangular and $\Pi$ a partial permutation with exactly $a$ ones.

quote.quote: Every rational $m\times m$ matrix $A$ of rank $a$ has a factorization

children.claim: The permutation $(H,D)\mapsto(H+AD,D)$ of address fields modulo $q^b$ is done with exactly $\operatorname{rank}(A)$ interchanges of $b$-digit fields plus $O(V)$ work, using triangular factors and controlled shifts.

quote.quote: can be performed with exactly $a$ interchanges of pairs of $b$-digit fields and $O(V)$ further work.

children.claim: The network makes $s<Wm$ calls on streams of volume $V/W$, so the per-volume cost obeys $F_k\le(s/W)F_{k-1}+O(1)$ with $s/W<m^\tau$, giving $F_k=O(e^\tau)$ at width $e=m^k$, scheduled depth first on fixed tapes.
children.salient: Each recursion level multiplies the cost per volume by $s/W$, which may exceed one, yet the total grows only like $e^\tau$ with $\tau<1$ because $s/W$ is strictly smaller than $m$, the factor by which the width grows.

quote.quote: For $a=s/W<m^\tau$ the geometric sum $\sum_{j=0}^k a^j$ is $O(m^{k\tau})$.

children.claim: Arbitrary widths and row counts reduce to power widths with enough rows, supplied by a few of the array's own high digits at cost below the final bound, so the interchange costs $O(Vu^\tau)$ for every $u$.

quote.quote: Rows for a general array can be supplied by a few of its own high digits.

children.claim: Digits in radix $2^b$ are placed on distinct prime cyclic axes, two source transforms (Gaussian resampling with chirp convolution over the ring via a twist) and one opposite transform give their convolution, and rescaling, rounding and carrying yield the exact $2n$-bit product.
children.method: Reduce the product to a radix-digit convolution, compute it with Fourier transforms made of Gaussian resampling, chirps and synthetic ring convolution, then recover exact integers

motivation.text: Multiplication is a convolution of the digit sequences, and a Fourier transform turns convolution into pointwise multiplication.

quote.quote: Splitting the inputs into radix digits reduces multiplication to convolution of short integer coefficients.

adds.name: precision
adds.meaning: The number of fractional bits of the fixed-point grid.

adds.name: axis count
adds.meaning: The number of axes (also the number of chunks a layer treats at once), a small power of $p$.

adds.name: chunk width
adds.meaning: The number of bits in one address chunk of a layer.

adds.name: log record length
adds.meaning: The base-two logarithm of the number of coefficients of a ring element.

adds.name: record length
adds.meaning: The number of complex coefficients of a polynomial modulo $y^r+1$.

adds.name: padded size
adds.meaning: The number of complex entries in the padded box of power-of-two axes.

adds.name: layer exponent
adds.meaning: A fixed exponent below one for the cost of a simultaneous butterfly layer.

adds.name: source product
adds.meaning: The product of the distinct odd prime lengths of the source axes.

adds.name: prime length
adds.meaning: The i-th prime source axis length, just below t_i.

adds.name: axis length
adds.meaning: The i-th power-of-two transform axis length, r/2 or r.

children.claim: Two forward synthetic transforms, a pointwise ring product by signed packing and the opposite transform give the normalized convolution $(f*g)/T$ over $\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$, with $T=rM$, error below $\sqrt2\,M(3\ell+1)2^{-p}$ and cost $O(Tp[dK+pK^{\tau-1}+\ell d^{\lambda'}+\log(rp)])$.
children.method: Apply the convolution theorem over the ring: transform both operands, multiply pointwise, transform back

motivation.text: Convolution becomes pointwise multiplication under a Fourier transform; over this ring the transform needs only signed shifts and the pointwise products are polynomial products done by the established multiplier.

children.claim: Placing the selected bits of the participating axes at a common offset in $K$-bit chunks lets every synthetic transform round use the simultaneous layer, so a transform of $T$ entries costs $O(Tp[dK+pK^{\tau-1}+\ell d^{\lambda'}])$.
children.method: Build the simultaneous layer, define the synthetic transform and its stored order, then lay out the axes so each round is one layer call

motivation.text: Each radix-two round must act on the same bit position of many axes at once for the layer to apply, so the axes' bits have to be brought to a common offset in consecutive chunks.

quote.quote: we must place the selected bits of the participating axes at a common offset in consecutive $K$-bit chunks.

children.salient: Each of the three cost terms $dK$, $pK^{\tau-1}$ and $\ell d^{\lambda'}$ is a power of $p$ below one after dividing by the volume, which is what makes the transform cheaper than $\Theta(Tp\ell)$.

children.claim: Applying $H_0(u,v)=((u+v)/2,(u-v)/2)$ at one common bit position of $D\le d$ address chunks of an array of $r$-coefficient polynomial records, then truncating once to the $2^{-p}$ grid, takes $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$ time with error below $\sqrt2\,2^{-p}$, rather than $D$ whole-array passes.
children.method: Write the layer as a tensor product of the two-point kernel $C$ through phase frames of the complex network, recurse on $e=mf$ axes with rank-deficit calls, make the basis changes by packed bit additions, and evaluate exactly in Gaussian dyadics before one truncation

motivation.text: The rank-deficit recursion that speeds up address interchange also applies to a network of two-point kernels; the layer must be evaluated exactly in dyadics because the intermediate operators are not contractions.

children.salient: One layer on $D$ chunks costs $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$ with $\lambda'<1$, which is less than the $D$ separate whole-array passes it replaces.

children.claim: A complex network with binary labels and Hadamard-conjugated phase frames $i^{\operatorname{wt}(P_Ux)}$ makes every edge a product of translation kernels $aI+bX_v$ and produces $C^{\otimes e}$ on every role, where $C=H\operatorname{diag}(1,i)H$, and $H_0=b\,\mathsf S C\mathsf S$.
children.salient: The same kernel $C$ appears on every role, scratch roles included, and the butterfly $H_0$ is just $C$ conjugated by the diagonal phases $\mathsf S=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)$ up to a scalar.

quote.quote: Proposition~\ref{prop:complex-motif-interface} therefore gives $C^{\otimes e}$ on every role, including roles whose initial scratch values were arbitrary.

children.claim: A binary row addition on corresponding selected bits of address chunks, which implements the binary basis changes, takes a constant number of whole-chunk cyclic shifts followed by repair of an explicitly bounded exceptional set of addresses.

quote.quote: The construction first uses a constant number of cyclic shifts of whole chunk ranges, then corrects an explicitly bounded set of addresses.

children.claim: A node of $e=m^k$ selected axes makes $s_{\rm c}<W_{\rm c}m$ recursive calls on slots of $e/m$ axes, each on a $1/W_{\rm c}$ share of the volume, so the same rank-deficit recursion gives cost $O(d^{\lambda'})$ per unit volume.

quote.quote: The phase construction supplies one recursive call on a slot for each vector in an edge residual basis, hence exactly \(s\) calls in one invocation of the network.

children.claim: Intermediate values of a butterfly layer are Gaussian integers over powers of two, computed exactly with a guard width of $O(d^{20})=o(p)$ extra bits, with a single truncation at the end.

quote.quote: The accelerated network is evaluated exactly until an entire normalized butterfly layer is complete.

children.claim: Every row of the layer matrix has absolute sum one, so the layer maps disk arrays to disk arrays and the single final truncation toward zero adds error below $\sqrt2\,2^{-p}$.

quote.quote: Thus $\mathcal H$ maps disk arrays to disk arrays, and componentwise truncation preserves that disk

children.claim: Over $\mathcal R_r=\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$ the normalized transforms $F_t^{-}$ and $F_t^{+}$ with roots of unity $\omega_t=y^{2r/t}$ are evaluated by radix-two butterfly rounds whose twiddle multiplications are signed shifts.
children.method: Run the radix-two decimation-in-frequency recursion with powers of $y$ as the roots of unity

motivation.text: Powers of $y$ serve as roots of unity and multiplication by such a root is a signed shift of the coefficient list.

quote.quote: Powers of $y$ then serve as roots of unity in the remaining axes, and multiplication by such a root is a signed shift of the coefficient list.

children.claim: In $\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$ with $y^r=-1$, multiplication by any power of $y$ permutes the coefficients and changes some signs, so it is a signed shift and an isometry for the maximum coefficient norm.

quote.quote: Multiplication by $y^a$, for any integer $a$, permutes the coefficients and changes some signs; consequently it is an isometry for this norm.

children.claim: Character sums of $\omega_t=y^{2r/t}$ vanish unless $t\mid j$, shown directly because the ring has zero divisors, so $F_t^+F_t^-=t^{-1}I$.

quote.quote: The ring has zero divisors, so we verify character cancellation directly instead of dividing by $\omega_t^j-1$.

children.claim: The map $H_0$, followed by multiplying one output by a power of $\omega_t$, splits a length-$t$ transform into two half-length transforms (decimation in frequency), and $\log_2 t$ rounds give the transform.

quote.quote: For $t\geq2$, the decimation-in-frequency step pairs $z_k$ with $z_{k+t/2}$ for $0\leq k<t/2$.

children.claim: The forward synthetic transform writes its outputs in bit-reversed slots, and the pointwise product and the opposite-sign transform consume that same order, so no reordering is executed.
children.salient: The bit-reversal permutation costs nothing, because the forward transform leaves frequencies in that order and the opposite transform is built to read them in that order.

quote.quote: The recursion writes its outputs directly in this order; it does not move whole frequency indices.

quote.quote: Each procedure has error less than $\sqrt2\ell\,2^{-p}$, returns disk grid coefficients in the same component format, and costs

children.claim: Evaluating polynomials at $2^{4p}$ (a signed Kronecker substitution) turns one product in the ring into four integer products by the established multiplier, and centered coefficients are read back, in $O(rp\log(rp))$ time.

quote.quote: One can compute the exact Gaussian integer numerators of $fg$, and then return $Q_p(fg/r)$ in that same format, in time $O(rp\log(rp))$ on a fixed number of tapes.

children.claim: Both forward transforms keep the layout order, the records are multiplied pointwise in that order, and the opposite transform followed by exact scaling by $M$ returns $\mathcal M_r(f,g)=(f*g)/T$.

quote.quote: Perform both forward transforms and retain their common $LB$ order.

children.claim: Gaussian resampling expresses the Fourier transform of length $s_i$ through a power-of-two length $t_i>s_i$ transform by contractions $A$ and $B_0$, with $P_{s_i}F_{s_i}=2^{2\alpha^2}B_0P_{t_i}F_{t_i}A$ and a small error $N-I$.
children.salient: The two coordinate permutations $P_{s_i}$ and $P_{t_i}$ stay inside the identity instead of being executed as sorts.

children.claim: The one-dimensional maps are applied one coordinate line at a time to a $d$-fold tensor, giving $RF_{\boldsymbol s}=2^\gamma\mathcal B_0QF_{\boldsymbol t}\mathcal A$ at line cost $O(dTp^{3/2+\delta}\alpha)$, with axis movement by the fast interchange.

quote.quote: For the tensor product, apply the one-dimensional maps to one coordinate line at a time.

children.claim: A Fourier transform is a pointwise phase multiplication, a cyclic convolution with a chirp array $a$, and another phase multiplication: $QF_{\boldsymbol t}u=\overline a\cdot(a*(\overline a\cdot u))/T$.

quote.quote: The factor $QF_{\boldsymbol t}$ in \eqref{eq:no-sort-tensor} can be computed from a cyclic convolution and two pointwise phase multiplications.

children.claim: The chirp absorbs the target permutation $Q$, and the source permutation $R$ cancels across two forward transforms, a pointwise product and the opposite transform: $(RF_{\boldsymbol s}^+)[(RF_{\boldsymbol s}u)\cdot(RF_{\boldsymbol s}v)]=(u*v)/S^2$.
children.salient: Neither coordinate permutation of resampling is ever executed: the target one is absorbed by the chirp and the source one cancels between the forward and opposite transforms.

quote.quote: The second identity shows how the retained source permutation $R$ cancels when computing a convolution.

children.claim: Taking $b=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$, $p=6b$, $d\approx b^\epsilon$, $K\approx d^c$, $T\approx n/b$ a power of two, axis lengths $t_i\in\{r/2,r\}$ and distinct odd primes $s_i$ just below $t_i$ with $T/2<S<T$ gives $Tp=\Theta(n)$ and $r$ larger than every power of $p$.

children.claim: Writing both inputs in radix $2^b$ with $q=\lceil n/b\rceil$ digits, the product coefficients are a cyclic convolution of length $S>2q-2$ with no wraparound and each coefficient is below $2^{3b}$.

quote.quote: Thus convolution modulo $x^S-1$ has no nonzero wraparound.

children.claim: For pairwise coprime lengths $s_i$ the map $x\mapsto\prod_i x_i^{\mu_i}$ turns a length-$S$ cyclic convolution into convolution on a product of prime cyclic axes, realized by triangular controlled shifts.
children.salient: Each new axis coordinate depends only on lower-index digits, so the whole change of order is a sequence of controlled cyclic shifts rather than a general sort.

quote.quote: Hence $\Phi$ is an isomorphism and preserves cyclic convolution.

children.claim: Multiplying coefficient $k$ by $\zeta^k$ with $\zeta=e^{\pi i/r}$ maps $\mathbb C[x]/(x^r-1)$ isomorphically onto $\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$, so negative wrap becomes cyclic wrap.
children.salient: A term that wraps past degree $r$ picks up $\zeta^r=-1$, which exactly cancels the sign $-1$ of the negacyclic wrap.

quote.quote: On the bases $(x_d^k)_{0\le k<r}$ and $(y^k)_{0\le k<r}$ it is diagonal, multiplying coefficient $k$ by the nonzero number $\zeta^k$.

children.claim: The digits are placed on the prime axes by $\Phi$, two source transforms and one opposite transform with a pointwise product give the digit convolution, and two exact rescalings by $S$ and $2^{2b+4}$ follow.

quote.quote: Apply the coefficient-address map $\Phi$, with its padded layout, to obtain source arrays $u,v$.

children.claim: Undoing the known scales $S$ and $2^{2b+4}$ leaves coefficient error below $1/2$, so rounding gives the exact integer coefficients and carry propagation in radix $2^b$ gives the exact $2n$-bit product.

quote.quote: The strict error below $1/2$ makes the nearest integer to that value the unique correct coefficient.

children.claim: Dividing each cost term by $Tp$ leaves powers of $p$ with margins $g_i$ below one; the smallest margin is $2\kappa=2^{-181}$, which absorbs any polylogarithmic factor and gives total time $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$.
children.salient: The smallest of the seven margins is $g_2=\epsilon c(1-\tau)=2^{-181}$, a product of tiny fixed parameters, which is why the final exponent $\kappa=2^{-182}$ is so small.

quote.quote: Thus $\min_i g_i=2^{-181}=2\kappa$.
